captured_redundancy_paragraph.text: In general, with K outcomes, the entropy is at most log two of K. The proof is one inequality. The log bends downward, so the average of logs is at most the log of the average: Jensen's inequality. Entropy is an average of logs. Swap in the log of the average, and the average of one over p is just the number of outcomes. So H is at most log K, with equality only when every outcome is equally likely. The gap measures structure a guesser can exploit. Shannon's redundancy is that gap divided by log two of K.

captured_autoregressive_pretraining_para.text: Here is why this matters for AI. Autoregressive language models are pretrained with this next-token loss: the average of log one over q, for each token of real text, given the tokens before it. Usually with the natural log, ln, so it's counted in nats: one nat is about 1.44 bits. It's the cross-entropy between the world's text and the model. Training can only shrink the divergence; the entropy of language itself is a floor no model can go below.
